newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan sends condolences over Deng, stocks bounce.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan sends condolences over Deng, stocks bounce.

text.p: Taiwan's presidential office sent its condolences on Thursday to the family of China's late paramount leader Deng Xiaoping and urged a "peaceful, cooperative, prosperous new era" between Taipei and Beijing.
But the island, which Beijing regards as a renegade province, maintained a military alert and advised its people to stay calm following Deng's death on Wednesday.

Taiwan share prices fell early in the day but closed 0.28 percent higher at 7,678.04 points after the government pledged to support the market and most investors appeared to shrug off news of Deng's death.
"Regarding Mr Deng Xiaoping's death, we hereby offer our condolences to his family," Huang Kun-huei, President Lee Teng-hui's chief of staff, said in a statement.

The foreign ministry said Taipei was "well prepared for contingencies" regarding political developments on the mainland, while the defence ministry said it had detected no unusual movements from Chinese troops.
Shi Hwei-you, vice-chairman of the cabinet's Mainland Affairs Council, said he hoped people would treat Deng's death calmly. The council formulates Taiwan's policies towards China.
"The government already has policies for post-Deng period. It will not change the policies," Shi told Reuters by telephone. He did not elaborate.
Taiwan and China have been diplomatic rivals since a Chinese civil war split them in 1949.
Beijing refuses to rule out the use of force to retake Taiwan. The island says it wants reunification, but insists this occur under democracy and a free market.
Taiwan media quoted military spokesman Kung Fan-ting as saying that the armed forces were on alert for any developments, but added the military had not yet raised its alert level.
"The situation on the mainland is likely to change, the armed forces will actively follow the current situation there," Kung said.
China's military held war games off the island in the run up to presidential polls in March last year in an exercise seen as trying to intimidate Taiwanese against voting for independence.
The presidential office's Huang praised Deng for launching economic reforms on the mainland which enhanced trade ties between Taiwan and China.

"Ever since Mr Deng Xiaoping's economic reforms, Taiwan's private sector has provided funds, technology and manpower to inject new life into mainland's economic development and raise its living standard," Huang said.
Some 30,000 Taiwan-funded businesses have invested an estimated US$20 billion in China since Taipei began allowing indirect contact with the mainland in the mid 1980s.

Government spokesman Su Chi said after a cabinet meeting that the government would launch stock market stabilisation measures and had prepared funds to support the bourse against any potential plunge.
The Taiwan dollar remained slightly lower at midday at T$27.597, recovered from a morning slump, against Wednesday's T$27.583 close.

Wu Hui-lin, senior economist at Chunghua Institution for Economic Research, said: "The market will fluctuate for a while to watch China's post-Deng development, but the impact won't be big as the market has reacted to Deng's death rumours several times before."
